title: First contact? Scientists discover first-ever direct radio signal from 'second Earth' beyond Solar System; what is Beta Pictoris b? - News24 Tech
excerpt: Scientists detected a radio signal from Beta Pictoris b, an exoplanet the constellation Pictor, about 63 million light years away.
content:
In a major discovery that could have potential implications on finding intelligent extraterrestrial life in the universe, researchers have detected the first-ever direct radio signal from a planet beyond our Solar System, sparking speculations whether it could be an attempt an intelligent species to establish contact with other advanced lifeforms.

What did scientists find?

According to Live Science, a team of scientists from the Harvard and Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics and the University of Oregon detected a radio signal from Beta Pictoris b, an exoplanet orbiting an A-type star in the constellation Pictor, about 63 million light years away.

Advertisment

The researchers observed “rapid, frequently recurring, and highly circularly polarized bursts (blows of strong radio waves), as well as continuous emission” at frequencies between 0.85 and 3.5 GHz, as per the report.

According to the research team, the telescope array focused on the star Beta Pictoris, which has three known planets orbiting it; Beta Pictoris b, Beta Pictoris c, and Beta Pictoris d. Observations revealed short, frequently recurring radio bursts, with radio waves largely circularly polarized, a characteristic feature of signals emitted by aurora borealis, they said.

“These are the same frequencies that were covered on four separate occasions in 2025 and 2026 using the MeerKAT radio telescope array in South Africa,” the scientists added.

Were the signals sent by an alien civilization?

No, while the radio signal is the first-ever to have come from an exoplanet, scientists believe it does not show any intelligent design, and was emitted by the planet’s auroras which are created when charged particles interact with atmospheric and magnetic field.

The energy is emitted in the form of radio waves, similar to auroras on Earth, which are visible as the northern and southern lights.

According to researchers, auroral radio bursts have been observed on planets in the solar system and some “ultra-cool dwarfs”, but never before has a radio signal been clearly detected from an extrasolar planet.

Notably, radio signals have previously been detected in planetary systems beyond our solar system, but it was not possible to determine with certainty whether the signals were coming from the planets or the stars they orbit.

What is Beta Pictoris b?

Discovered in 2008 via direct imaging, Beta Pictoris has been dubbed as a ‘super Earth’, though the moniker is a misnomer because it is actually a gas giant that closely resembles Jupiter rather than our blue planet.

Beta Pictoris b is roughly 10 to 11.7 times the mass of Jupiter and slightly larger in radius, and takes just 8-9 hours to rotate on its axis, which is believed to be the reason for its auroral radio emissions. The exoplanet has a strong magnetic, estimated to be thousands of times stronger than that of the Earth.

“This is the first direct measurement of an exoplanet’s magnetic field strength and it matches dynamo-scaling estimates for a young, large, and massive planet,” according to the researchers.
